question.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2-2x_1x_2+2x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/4ac94173e3fced93071a8677fb1f4d94d34cdac55c8c479f7bb1e1c3f3b955e2.svg)

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +3 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/f2771161cd2e0bd19da05e295acf6c92ff9db0d78cde40dfa94d127e19793741.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/6dbc527fa88e22649a134021e20e3d3e9cb23622d944a2e372eee1d706517c7b.svg)

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/ac8122ec6c639a712defa83c8f52b7593a517e961d210949983dbd994b361079.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/7c15edf59391b4e12818a0efd96b035740aa10f80fa64e7a91d4932d22f6ba75.svg)

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/22a17feb35e9fb1b0ff14a6091e1baba685e3ec5809374a308861cb90bd3c0f1.svg)
